transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Nguyen (Redwood SE), Tom Keegan (Ironcrest SRE), Priya Bhandari (Ironcrest Platform Eng), James Li (Ironcrest Sec Ops)
Shared artifacts: signed-bundle-template.tar.gz (link shared in chat), perf-spreadsheet-ironcrest-2026.xlsx (link), runbook-draft.md (link)

Summary (auto):
- Walkthrough of offline bundle creation and verification, including code signing and sha256 manifests.
- Discussed license rotation for air-gapped clusters and short-lived on-device tokens.
- Kernel/driver compatibility matrix review; DKMS vs static modules; firmware notes.
- KV cache prefetch/warmup approaches: lazy vs aggressive prefetch and eviction tuning.
- Batching: continuous batching configuration to meet 95th percentile latency SLOs; quantization tradeoffs for throughput.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Okay everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE on the account. Carlos will do most of the deep tech, um quick role call?
[00:08] Tom Keegan: Tom here, SRE at Ironcrest.
[00:10] Priya Bhandari: Priya, platform engineering.
[00:12] James Li: James, security.
[00:14] Carlos Nguyen: Carlos, Redwood SE. Hey.
[00:16] Maya Patel: Great. Goal today is to nail down the offline artifact flow and the runtime tuning knobs you should change on arrival, especially around KV warmup and batching.

[00:45] Carlos Nguyen: Quick note, when we say "bundle" we're talking about a tar that contains signed model artifacts, runtime binaries, a manifest.json with sha256 checksums and a license file that includes an offline token. In air-gapped flow we strongly recommend signing the tar with an attestation key and including an accompanying .sig file so your ops team can verify via our public key.
[01:10] Tom Keegan: On the signing, can you clarify—if we do our own signing pipeline, is Redwood's public key still required to verify runtime compatibility, or can we trust only our internal CA? 
[01:22] Carlos Nguyen: Good question. For the runtime to auto-accept the bundle when it's imported, the installer checks signatures against a list of trusted keys. You can add your internal CA to the trust store, but for license rotation we include metadata signed by Redwood to assert entitlement. If you want fully self-contained, we can provide an enterprise mode that accepts your CA but then we need to exchange key fingerprints over a secure channel.
[01:45] James Li: That exchange process — we need to get that through SecOps. Is there a documented attestation flow?
[01:52] Maya Patel: Yes, Carlos has a runbook draft, we shared runbook-draft.md in chat. It includes key exchange steps and an HSM-backed option for signing if you want to rotate keys without re-issuing bundles.

[02:25] Priya Bhandari: On the license tokens, what are the TTLs we can expect? We can't have tokens that need daily rotation if shipments take several days.
[02:34] Carlos Nguyen: We support several patterns: long-lived device keys baked into the image for one-year leases, or short-lived tokens rotated via an offline rotation manifest. For airgap, typical pattern is a rotation manifest that contains a small set of one-time use tokens signed by your CA — you import that manifest during transport and the node consumes tokens on first boot. TTLs are configurable per-customer; recommend at least 30-day windows if shipping times are unpredictable.

[03:05] Tom Keegan: Ok that sounds workable. Now, GPU drivers — we've had trouble when the kernel is updated and modules don't match. Does Redwood require a specific driver set? What's your recommended approach for kernel-module signing etc?
[03:18] Carlos Nguyen: We maintain a compatibility matrix. For A100 clusters we recommend R515+ driver baseline and matching cuda 12.x builds. For offline installs, two approaches: provide prebuilt kernel modules signed for the target kernel or install DKMS so modules rebuild on boot. DKMS is flexible but can be brittle if you have a custom kernel. If you have strict change control, packaging signed modules per kernel (and including the signature) is more deterministic. Also, for FIPS/HSM environments you may need to do module signing; we include guidance for generating module-sign keys and how to add them to /etc/modprobe.d.
[04:00] James Li: Module signing — does Redwood provide signed modules, or do we sign them?
[04:04] Carlos Nguyen: Redwood can provide vendor-signed modules as an enterprise add-on, or we hand off the module sources and you can sign them with your internal key during image build.

[04:34] Priya Bhandari: A specific pain: KV cache warmup. At scale when we spin up 100s of workers we see cold starts with high tail latency. Any patterns?
[04:45] Carlos Nguyen: Yes. There are two axis: logical (what prompts are hot) and physical (how the runtime warms GPU memory). For the KV cache we recommend a staggered prefetch where the control plane sends lightweight prefix requests to populate per-shard KV entries before accepting traffic. For sequence-heavy workloads, pre-populating the KV for common prefixes reduces tail. Implementation options: run a background warmup job in each node that replays representative prompts, or use a coordinated warmup where one node primes a shared artifact and others fetch via intra-cluster fetch. Note in air-gapped mode the intra-node fetch is local only.
[05:25] Tom Keegan: Wouldn't replaying prompts be noisy and expensive?
[05:28] Carlos Nguyen: It can be. Another approach is to serialize and ship a snapshot of the KV cache as part of the bundle — we support a kv-snapshot.bin format that can be loaded at startup. Tradeoffs: snapshot size can be large depending on context length. Often a hybrid works: snapshot of top-level tokens + lightweight replay of high-frequency prefixes.
[05:50] Priya Bhandari: How large are these snapshots usually?
[05:53] Carlos Nguyen: For our typical 2k context models, snapshots for a shard are in the 200–800MB range depending on caching granularity. You'll want to size your transport media accordingly.

[06:20] Maya Patel: Quick note on quantization — we recommended 4-bit quant in other customers but you've got some long-tail legal language so we want to confirm quality. What accuracy hit can we expect?
[06:30] Carlos Nguyen: With our tuned Q4 profiles, you generally see sub-1% delta on common NLU tasks, but for specific domain-sensitive prompts there can be regressions. We suggest running a small eval prompt set (we can provide) against float32, int8 and q4 to measure per-instruction/regression. If you need absolute parity, keep a float or int8 fallback and route a small sampling to it.

[06:58] James Li: Routing to fallback models in air-gapped — how does the failover work?
[07:02] Carlos Nguyen: The runtime supports policy-based fallback — if a q4 model's perplexity or safety check fails or latency is too high, it can automatically reroute to a pinned float variant. That logic lives entirely on-device, so air-gapped clusters are supported.

[07:40] Tom Keegan: Batching config. Our SLO is 95th < 200ms for short completion requests (avg 64 tokens). We want throughput of ~300 TPS across the pool during peak. How do we tune?
[07:52] Carlos Nguyen: Continuous batching and adaptive batch windows are key. Set a max batch size based on GPU memory (we can compute), and a batch wait time (the micro-window). For low-latency SLOs you set micro-window to 6–12ms and a max batch age of 20–30ms. Also enable per-token preemption for high-priority requests. Another lever is model shard allocation: leave some dedicated low-latency capacity (small batch, low-concurrency) and a larger pool for throughput (higher batch).
[08:30] Priya Bhandari: Can Redwood's autoscaler respect this split?
[08:33] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, you can configure node pools with labels (latency-tier=low/high) and autoscaler policies per pool. In Dedicated/Private mode we expose that in the config.

[09:05] Maya Patel: We're near the top of the hour; let's go through an example end-to-end: packaging, transport, verification, install, then a warmup and perf run. Carlos do the steps?
[09:14] Carlos Nguyen: Sure. Step 1: Build artifacts on an isolated build host. Output includes model-* files, runtime-binaries.tgz, kv-snapshot.bin (optional), manifest.sha256, bundle.sig, license.manifest.json. Step 2: Transfer via approved media — we recommend writing to a single-drive tar with checksum verified post-write using sha256sum -c manifest.sha256. Step 3: At the receiving datacenter, verify signatures and checksums, check policy (operator step). Step 4: Install the driver RPMs included or run DKMS. Step 5: Import bundle into runtime with --verify-signature flag and specify trust store. Step 6: Run warmup job: either load kv-snapshot or run the warmup playback. Step 7: Run smoke perf tests (the perf spreadsheet has the commands).
[10:10] Tom Keegan: On the install step, if a module fails DKMS build due to missing kernel headers, should we stop the install? We have strict change control but want automation.
[10:21] Carlos Nguyen: Best practice is to fail safe — if kernel headers mismatch, abort and surface the error. But you can ship a prebuilt module as fallback. Automating a build in a constrained environment is risky.

[10:50] Priya Bhandari: For the perf run, can we get a lightweight harness that hits the runtime locally, simulating 64-token completions with 100 concurrent clients?
[10:58] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we have a stress harness script we can provide. We'll parameterize concurrency and sequence length. We'll also add a KV warmup step so you can compare cold vs warmed tail.

[11:20] James Li: Security question: how do we reconcile supply chain guarantees if we accept vendor-signed modules?
[11:26] Carlos Nguyen: You can require a signed supply chain attestation bundle that includes build provenance (SBOM-like) and signature timestamps. For high-security, we recommend storing module signatures and verifying in a hardened enclave or using the HSM-backed signing flow.

[11:50] Maya Patel: Alright let's capture next steps — Carlos will share the signed-bundle-template and the harness; Tom/Priya will run the noted perf and report; James will coordinate SecOps for the key exchange.

[12:08] Tom Keegan: Quick clarifying Q: If we choose kv-snapshot strategy, how is version compatibility handled? If model updates change the KV schema, will the snapshot still load?
[12:18] Carlos Nguyen: Good call-out. Snapshots are versioned with the model build id and runtime version in manifest. If incompatible, the runtime refuses to load and falls back to replay warmup. We'll add a post-install check that validates snapshot/model/runtime compatibility before import.

[12:48] Priya Bhandari: Anything about transport integrity for large drives? We use encrypted hardware drives but need chain-of-custody steps.

[12:54] Maya Patel: We'll propose a chain-of-custody template with signature steps: hash on write, witness signature, sealed drives, and verification on receipt. We'll drop a template in the runbook.

[13:20] Carlos Nguyen: One more practical tip: compressing kv-snapshots with zstd --ultra --22 gives good size reduction without heavy CPU cost during load. Also split snapshots per-shard so parallel loads happen during startup.

[13:42] James Li: Noted. Also ask: do you support entropy for offline license rotation — like the tokens being consumed in strictly increasing counters? We want replay protection.

[13:51] Carlos Nguyen: Yes tokens include nonce and monotonic counters; the runtime persists last-seen counters in a protected store so replay is prevented.

[14:10] Maya Patel: Moving to wrap — let's confirm deadlines. Carlos will share artifacts by Friday (Nov 6). Tom/Priya aim to run perf by Nov 10. We'll target a rehearsal week of Nov 16. James to confirm SecOps channel for key exchange by Nov 9.

[14:32] Carlos Nguyen: I'll attach a small checklist in the Slack thread after this call: build host checklist, manifest template, and driver RPM naming conventions.

[14:45] Tom Keegan: Awesome. One last thing — did you mention a mode for on-device fallback to a smaller quantized model if memory pressure spikes?
[14:53] Carlos Nguyen: Yes, we support tiered model variants with local routing; runtime will evict large model shard pages and load a smaller quant variant. That adds a cold load penalty but keeps availability.

[15:08] Priya Bhandari: Great, thanks everyone.
[15:10] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts and runbook updates.
